doc.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Chicago childhood: theaters, violin and first bass
title: The Vendome versus the Grand: Erskine Tate and Dave Payton
summary: The Vendome Theater had Louis Armstrong and Eddie South, while Dave Payton's Grand stayed anti-jazz and concert-minded, which Taylor links to color prejudice.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Really? What do you mean, what kind of revolution?
Well Chicago, they had… all the people that came up from the South… you‟ve got the Vind Dome Theater. Do you know about the Vind Dome Theater?
With [Unintelligible} band, with Louis Armstrong in there and Eddie South and Jimmy Bertrame, all [unintelligible].
Now is that the biggest black theater?
The black theater and it was just fabulous. Across the street was the Grand Theater that had Dave Payton but they were more classical, they were more minstrel type of playing.
Really? The difference in Payton… what did they play? You say classical, in what respect?
They played things like Willie Woogies stuff of…
So really more in the European… based on the European models?

Oh, yeah. And then Dave Payton was the pianist and absolutely anti-jazz. He was not for syncopation at all. He wanted to play melodic things and they did just that in their tuxedos and really… [Unintelligible] band, even though they were just in tuxedos. But they played the overtures. After the movie was over there was an overture [unintelligible] something like that. Then they went into My Daddy Rocks Me and One Steady Road, and Eddie South was playing solo and Louis Armstrong would play a solo, and every Sunday my mother would take me [unintelligible] to 15th, 14th to see this. All people of any kind of stature at all would try to get down to the Vind Dome Theater on a Sunday to see this marvelous show.
Social, yeah, it was a social and it was really… you got both sides of it. But Dave Payton, he [unintelligible] Chicago with a [unintelligible] and he was now complete anti-jazz.

Well that‟s sort of like what you were talking about with the color discrimination between black people. It was the same thing where you wanted not only to look white but you wanted to play white music or music that was acceptable to white people and so forth.
So it was a whole dichotomy in that area where many people felt to get ahead you had to be more like white then like black.
